How it works: Replace the negative ない (nai) with ず (zu). This is the classical/literary negative conjunctive form, meaning 'without doing'. It's equivalent to modern ないで (naide).

Example from this song: 構わず (kamawazu) = 'without caring' — from 構う (kamau, 'to care/mind') → 構わない (kamawanai, negative) → 構わず (kamawazu)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べず (tabezu, 'without eating')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わず (iwazu, 'without saying')
• する (suru, 'to do') → せず (sezu, 'without doing')

Note: する → せず (not しず) is an irregular form to memorize. ず is common in written Japanese, formal speech, proverbs, and anime lyrics. 振り向かず進む (furimukazu susumu, 'advance without looking back').

How it works: Add ぜ (ze) at the end of a sentence for strong masculine assertion. It conveys confidence, excitement, and determination. Very common in hip-hop and shonen anime.

Example from this song: いいぜ (ii ze) = 'It's good!' / 行くぜ (iku ze) = 'Let's go!' — ぜ turns statements into confident declarations.

More examples:
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やるぜ (yaru ze, 'I'll do it, yeah!')
• 負けない (makenai, 'won't lose') → 負けないぜ (makenai ze, 'I won't lose!')
• 最高 (saikou, 'the best') → 最高だぜ (saikou da ze, 'It's the best!')

Note: ぜ is strongly masculine and casual. Using it in formal settings would be inappropriate. In this hip-hop track, it perfectly matches the high-energy, confident tone. Strength ranking: ぞ (strongest) > ぜ > よ (mildest).

How it works: Attach そう (sō) to the verb stem (masu-stem) to express that something appears about to happen based on visual evidence — 'it looks like it will X'.

Example from this song: 途切れそうだ (togiresō da) = 'seems about to break off' — from 途切れる (togireru, 'to be interrupted') → 途切れ (togire, stem) + そうだ (sō da, 'seems like')

More examples:
• 降る (furu, 'to rain') → 降りそうだ (furisō da, 'looks like it'll rain')
• 壊れる (kowareru, 'to break') → 壊れそうだ (kowaresō da, 'looks about to break')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣きそうだ (nakisō da, 'looks about to cry')

Note: This そう is based on appearance/observation. Different from hearsay そうだ (after dictionary form): 雨が降るそうだ (ame ga furu sō da, 'I heard it will rain'). For adjectives: drop い, add そう: 美味しい → 美味しそう (oishisō, 'looks delicious').

How it works: Combine a verb's te-form with いた (ita, past of いる) to express a state or action that was ongoing in the past. It's like English 'was doing' or 'had been doing.'

Example from this song: 立ち尽くしていた (tachitsukushite ita) = 'was standing frozen' — from 立ち尽くす (tachitsukusu, 'to stand rooted to the spot')

More examples:
• 食べていた (tabete ita, 'was eating') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 待っていた (matte ita, 'was waiting') — from 待つ (matsu, 'to wait')
• 雨が降っていた (ame ga futte ita, 'it was raining') — from 降る (furu, 'to fall/rain')

Note: In casual speech, ていた contracts to てた (teta). In the song, 立ち尽くしてた (tachitsukushiteta) is this casual contraction.

How it works: Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb and add いる (iru). This expresses an ongoing action or a resulting state. In casual speech, いる is often shortened to る.

Example from this song: えがいてる (egaiteru) = 'is drawing/imagining' — from えがく (egaku, 'to draw/imagine') → えがいて (egaite, te-form) + いる (iru) → えがいてる (casual contraction)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べている (tabete iru, 'is eating') → 食べてる (tabeteru, casual)
• 住む (sumu, 'to live') → 住んでいる (sunde iru, 'is living/lives') → 住んでる (sunderu, casual)
• 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知っている (shitte iru, 'knows') → 知ってる (shitteru, casual)

Note: The casual contraction dropping い is very common in songs and everyday speech. ている can indicate either an action in progress or a state that has resulted from a completed action.

name: 〜てくれ (te kure: do it for me! / please do)

explanation.en:
How it works: くれ (kure) is the imperative of くれる (kureru, 'to do for me'). Attach it to a verb's te-form for a rough/casual request: 'do this for me!'

Example from this song: 聞いてくれ (kiite kure) = 'listen to me!' — from 聞く (kiku, 'to listen') → 聞いて (kiite) + くれ (kure)

More examples:
• 見てくれ (mite kure, 'look at this!') — from 見る (miru, 'to see')
• 信じてくれ (shinjite kure, 'believe me!') — from 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe')
• 待ってくれ (matte kure, 'wait for me!') — from 待つ (matsu, 'to wait')

Note: てくれ is more direct/rough than てください. It's masculine and common in punk, rock, and emotional contexts. Adding よ softens it slightly: 聞いてくれよ (kiite kure yo).

Expresses supposition or probability: "probably" or "I think." It is the polite form of だろう (darou).

How it works:
Attach でしょう (deshou) after the plain form of a verb, adjective, or noun.

Example from this song:
忘れたのでしょう (wasureta no deshou, "You’ve probably forgotten")

More examples:
- 明日は雨でしょう (ashita wa ame deshou, "It will probably rain tomorrow")
- 彼は来ないでしょう (kare wa konai deshou, "He probably won’t come")
- 大丈夫でしょう (daijoubu deshou, "It’s probably fine")

How it works:
な-adjectives (na-adjectives) connect to nouns using な (na). Unlike い-adjectives (i-adjectives) which directly modify nouns, な-adjectives need this な (na) particle between them and the noun. This is one of the first patterns learners encounter.

Example from this song:
大切な物 (taisetsu na mono) — "important thing"
大切 (taisetsu, "important/precious") needs な (na) before the noun 物 (mono, "thing").

More examples:
• 静かな夜 (shizuka na yoru) — "a quiet night"
• 好きな食べ物 (suki na tabemono) — "favorite food"
• 元気な子供 (genki na kodomo) — "an energetic child"

How it works: Take the ない-form, add で (de), then いて (ite, te-form of いる). This requests someone to maintain a negative state — 'keep not doing X' or 'stay in the state of not having done X'.

Example from this song: 閉ざさないでいて (tozasanaide ite) = 'keep it from closing / stay open' — from 閉ざす (tozasu, 'to close off') → 閉ざさない (tozasanai, negative) + でいて (de ite, 'keep being')

More examples:
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れないでいて (wasurenaide ite, 'keep not forgetting / don't forget')
• 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わらないでいて (kawaranaide ite, 'keep not changing / stay the same')
• 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up') → 諦めないでいて (akiramenaide ite, 'keep not giving up')

Note: This is more specific than just ないで (naide, 'don't'). The いて adds 'stay in that state' — it's a request for ongoing non-action, not just a one-time prohibition.

How it works: Shorten なくてはいけない (nakute wa ikenai, 'must do') to the casual なくちゃ (nakucha). This expresses obligation or necessity in a conversational way.

Example from this song: 信じられなくちゃ (shinjirarena kucha) = 'I have to be able to believe' — from 信じられる (shinjirareru, 'can believe') → 信じられない (shinjiranai, negative) → 信じられなくちゃ (shinjirarena kucha, 'must be able to believe')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かなくちゃ (ikanakucha, 'I have to go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べなくちゃ (tabenakucha, 'I have to eat')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しなくちゃ (shinakucha, 'I have to do it')

Note: Contraction chain: なくてはいけない → なくては → なくちゃ → なきゃ (even shorter). All mean 'must/have to'. なくちゃ is the most common casual form. It's warm and conversational.

How it works: Add のさ (no sa) at the end of a sentence to provide an explanation with casual, often masculine emphasis. の (no) is the explanatory particle and さ (sa) adds assertion.

Example from this song: The song uses のさ to assert explanations in a laid-back, confident way — 'that's just how it is, you see'.

More examples:
• そう (sou, 'that's right') → そうなのさ (sou na no sa, 'that's just how it is')
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなのさ (suki na no sa, 'it's that I like it, you see')
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かるのさ (wakaru no sa, 'I understand, you know')

Note: のさ is more casual and assertive than のだ or んだ. It's common in song lyrics and casual male speech. The feminine equivalent would be のよ (no yo).

How it works: This cleft sentence structure emphasizes one part of the sentence. Verb + のは (no wa) turns the action into a topic, and だ (da) identifies it. Pattern: 'The thing that does X is Y.'

Example from this song: 僕を強くするのは仲間の絆 (boku o tsuyoku suru no wa nakama no kizuna) = 'what makes me strong is the bond with my companions' — the のは highlights 'the thing that makes me strong'

More examples:
• 好きなのは音楽だ (suki na no wa ongaku da, 'what I like is music') — emphasizing the object
• 大切なのは気持ちだ (taisetsu na no wa kimochi da, 'what's important is feelings') — emphasizing importance
• 教えてくれたのは先生だ (oshiete kureta no wa sensei da, 'the one who taught me was the teacher') — emphasizing the person

Note: の nominalizes the verb clause (turns it into a noun phrase). This structure is used when you want to say 'the one who / the thing that / what...'

name: 〜はずなのに (hazu nanoni: should be, but...)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine はず (hazu, 'should be') + なのに (nanoni, 'despite that') to express disappointment that reality differs from expectation — 'it should be X, and yet...'.

Example from this song: 知ったはずなのに (shitta hazu nanoni) = 'I should have known, but...' — from 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知った (shitta, past) + はず (hazu, 'should') + なのに (nanoni, 'and yet')

More examples:
• 終わる (owaru, 'to end') → 終わったはずなのに (owatta hazu nanoni, 'it should have ended, but...')
• 幸せ (shiawase, 'happy') → 幸せなはずなのに (shiawase na hazu nanoni, 'I should be happy, but...')
• できる (dekiru, 'can do') → できるはずなのに (dekiru hazu nanoni, 'I should be able to, but...')

Note: This pattern beautifully captures emotional conflict. はず = confident expectation. なのに = the reality contradicts it. Together they express frustration, sadness, or confusion.

How it works: Change the verb ending to create an 'if' condition. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with れば. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent and add ば.

Example from this song: 過ぎれば (sugireba) = 'if it passes / if you go too far' — from 過ぎる (sugiru, 'to pass/exceed') → 過ぎれば (sugireba, 'if it passes')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行けば (ikeba, 'if you go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat')
• 高い (takai, 'expensive') → 高ければ (takakereba, 'if it's expensive')

Note: For い-adjectives, change い to ければ. For godan verbs: く→けば, む→めば, す→せば, つ→てば, ぬ→ねば, ぶ→べば, る→れば.

How it works: みたいに (mitai ni) means 'like' or 'similar to.' It's the adverbial form of みたい, used to compare actions or states. Attach it to nouns or plain form verbs.

Example from this song: The song uses みたいに to compare the singer's situation to something familiar — creating a vivid image.

More examples:
• 鳥みたいに飛びたい (tori mitai ni tobitai, 'want to fly like a bird') — from 鳥 (tori, 'bird')
• 子供みたいに遊ぶ (kodomo mitai ni asobu, 'play like a child') — from 子供 (kodomo, 'child')
• 嘘みたいに消えた (uso mitai ni kieta, 'disappeared as if it were a lie') — from 嘘 (uso, 'lie')

Note: みたいに is the casual equivalent of のように (no you ni). Use みたいに in speech and songs, のように in writing and formal contexts. Both mean 'like/as if.'

name: 〜ようとする (you to suru) — try to / about to

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb volitional form + とする (to suru) means "to try to ~" or "to be about to ~." The volitional form expresses intention (行こう, ikou, "let's go"), and adding とする (to suru) shows the attempt or the moment just before the action. It captures effort and intention, especially when the outcome is uncertain.

Example from this song:
挑もうとする (idomou to suru) — "trying to challenge"
The singer is making an effort to face a difficult challenge head-on.

More examples:
• 逃げようとしたが捕まった (nigeyou to shita ga tsukamatta) — "tried to escape but was caught"
• 寝ようとしている (neyou to shite iru) — "is trying to sleep"
• 立ち上がろうとする (tachiagaro to suru) — "tries to stand up"

How it works: Add んだよ (nda yo) at the end of a sentence to strongly explain or emphasize something. ん (n) is the contracted explanatory の (no), だ (da) is the copula, and よ (yo) adds assertive emphasis.

Example from this song: The song uses んだよ to assert emotional truths with feeling — 'that's the way it is!' or 'I'm telling you that...'.

More examples:
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなんだよ (suki nandayo, 'I'm telling you, I like it!')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くんだよ (iku ndayo, 'I'm going, you know!')
• 大丈夫 (daijoubu, 'fine') → 大丈夫なんだよ (daijoubu nandayo, 'I'm telling you, it's fine!')

Note: んだよ is casual and direct. It's warmer than plain よ because の/ん adds the feeling of 'let me explain why'. After な-adjectives and nouns, add な before んだよ.

How it works: Attach 次第 (shidai) to a noun to mean 'depending on' or 'up to'. It can also attach to verb masu-stem to mean 'as soon as'.

Example from this song: 自分次第 (jibun shidai) = 'up to yourself / depends on you' — from 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') + 次第 (shidai, 'depending on')

More examples:
• 天気 (tenki, 'weather') → 天気次第 (tenki shidai, 'depending on the weather')
• 気持ち (kimochi, 'feelings') → 気持ち次第 (kimochi shidai, 'depends on how you feel')
• 届く (todoku, 'to arrive') → 届き次第 (todoki shidai, 'as soon as it arrives')

Note: Noun + 次第 = 'depends on'. Verb masu-stem + 次第 = 'as soon as'. 結果次第 (kekka shidai, 'depending on the results'). This is a common business/formal expression that also appears in motivational contexts.

How it works: Change a verb to express ability — 'can do X'. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with られる. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent and add る.

Example from this song: しゃべれた (shabereta) = 'was able to talk' — from しゃべる (shaberu, 'to talk') → しゃべれる (shabereru, 'can talk') → しゃべれた (shabereta, 'was able to talk')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べられる (taberareru, 'can eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行ける (ikeru, 'can go')
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') → 読める (yomeru, 'can read')

Note: For godan verbs: く→ける, す→せる, つ→てる, む→める, ぶ→べる, ぬ→ねる, う→える, る→れる. In casual speech, 食べられる is often shortened to 食べれる (tabereru) — called ら抜き (ra-nuki).
Adding 合う to a verb stem creates a reciprocal: 向き合う ('face each other'), 助け合う ('help each other'), 分かり合う ('understand each other'), 愛し合う ('love each other'). Productive — works on most action verbs.
explanation.es: Añadir 合う a la raíz verbal forma recíprocos: 向き合う, 助け合う, 分かり合う, 愛し合う. Patrón productivo.
explanation.pt-BR: Acrescentar 合う à raiz verbal cria um recíproco: 向き合う, 助け合う, 分かり合う, 愛し合う. Padrão produtivo.

explanation.en: い-adjectives drop い → ければ (赤い → 赤ければ); verbs change ending to え-row + ば (傷つく → 傷つけば, 流す → 流せば, 失う → 失えば). 〜ば is a more general/hypothetical conditional than 〜たら (concrete event-based) or なら (assuming X is true).
explanation.es: Los adjetivos い pierden la い → ければ (赤い → 赤ければ); verbos cambian la terminación a fila え + ば (傷つく → 傷つけば). 〜ば es más general/hipotético que 〜たら o なら.
explanation.pt-BR: Adjetivos い perdem o い → ければ (赤い → 赤ければ); verbos mudam terminação para fileira え + ば (傷つく → 傷つけば). 〜ば é mais geral/hipotético que 〜たら ou なら.

explanation.en:
〜きれない is the negative of 〜きる. The suffix 切る (kiru) attached to a verb's i-stem means 'do (X) completely / through to the end'; negating it (〜きれない) means 'cannot do (X) fully'. Literary form: 〜きれぬ.

This song uses 隠しきれない気持ち ('feelings I can't quite hide') and 数えきれぬ星 ('uncountable stars' — literary 〜ぬ). The 〜きれない / 〜きれぬ pair captures emotional and quantitative overflow.

Other typical examples: 食べきれない ('I can't finish eating'), 数えきれない ('countless'), 言いきれない ('I can't say definitively'), 待ちきれない ('I can't wait any longer').

Expresses a strong preference: "rather than doing X (which is undesirable), I would choose Y instead." The speaker considers X so bad that anything else is better.

How it works:
Attach ぐらいなら (gurai nara) after the dictionary form of a verb. The clause that follows states the preferred alternative.

Example from this song:
傷ついた足を休ませるぐらいなら (kizutsuita ashi o yasumaseru gurai nara, "Rather than resting your wounded legs...")

More examples:
- 嘘をつくぐらいなら黙ったほうがいい (uso o tsuku gurai nara damatta hou ga ii, "Rather than lie, it's better to stay silent")
- 諦めるぐらいなら最後まで戦う (akirameru gurai nara saigo made tatakau, "Rather than give up, I'll fight to the end")
- 待つぐらいなら自分で行く (matsu gurai nara jibun de iku, "Rather than wait, I'll go myself")

name: 〜ことない (koto nai) — absence of experience or action

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb plain form + ことない (koto nai) or ことがない (koto ga nai) means "there is no ~ / never ~." When it uses past tense + ことがない (koto ga nai), it means "have never done ~": 行ったことがない (itta koto ga nai, "have never been"). こと (koto) nominalizes the verb into a concept, and ない (nai) negates it.

Example from this song:
変わることない過去 (kawaru koto nai kako) — "the past that doesn't change"
The past is something that never changes — an immutable fact.

More examples:
• 日本に行ったことがない (nihon ni itta koto ga nai) — "I have never been to Japan"
• 泣くことなんてない (naku koto nante nai) — "there's no need to cry"
• 諦めることはない (akirameru koto wa nai) — "there's no reason to give up"

How it works: Create the causative form to mean 'make/let someone do something'. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with させる. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its あ-row equivalent and add せる.

Example from this song: 払わせる (harawaseru) = 'make them pay' — from 払う (harau, 'to pay') → 払わ (harawa, あ-row) + せる (seru) = 払わせる (harawaseru)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べさせる (tabesaseru, 'make/let eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かせる (ikaseru, 'make/let go')
• 飲む (nomu, 'to drink') → 飲ませる (nomaseru, 'make/let drink')

Note: For godan verbs: う→わせる, く→かせる, す→させる, つ→たせる, む→ませる. Whether it means 'make' (force) or 'let' (allow) depends on context. する → させる, 来る → 来させる (kosaseru).

How it works: Place しか (shika) after a verb in dictionary form, followed by ない (nai). This means 'there is no choice but to' or 'can only'. しか always requires a negative verb.

Example from this song: 進むしかない (susumu shika nai) = 'there is no choice but to move forward' — from 進む (susumu, 'to advance') + しか (shika, 'nothing but') + ない (nai, 'not')

More examples:
• 待つ (matsu, 'to wait') → 待つしかない (matsu shika nai, 'can only wait')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じるしかない (shinjiru shika nai, 'have no choice but to believe')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やるしかない (yaru shika nai, 'just gotta do it')

Note: This grammar conveys resignation mixed with determination. The speaker acknowledges limited options but accepts what must be done. It's commonly used in both spoken and written Japanese to express resolve.

How it works: そう (sou) after a verb's masu-stem or adjective stem means 'looks like' or 'seems about to.' Add な (na) to modify a noun.

Example from this song: 張り裂けそうな (harisakesou na) = 'about to burst / looks like it will tear apart' — from 張り裂ける (harisakeru, 'to burst/tear') → 張り裂け (harisake, stem) + そうな (sou na)

More examples:
• 泣きそう (nakisou, 'about to cry') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry')
• おいしそうな料理 (oishisou na ryouri, 'delicious-looking food') — from おいしい (oishii, 'delicious')
• 降りそうな空 (furisou na sora, 'sky that looks like it'll rain') — from 降る (furu, 'to rain')

Note: Verb stem + そう = 'looks like it's about to.' Adjective stem + そう = 'looks/seems (quality).' Exception: いい → よさそう (yosasou), ない → なさそう (nasasou). Add な before nouns, に before verbs.

How it works: Add ために (tame ni) after a verb in dictionary form to express purpose — 'in order to do X'. For nouns, use noun + のために (no tame ni).

Example from this song: 飛び越えるために (tobikoeru tame ni) = 'in order to leap over' — from 飛び越える (tobikoeru, 'to leap over') + ために (tame ni, 'in order to')

More examples:
• 勝つ (katsu, 'to win') → 勝つために (katsu tame ni, 'in order to win')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べるために (taberu tame ni, 'in order to eat')
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢のために (yume no tame ni, 'for the sake of a dream')

Note: ために can also express cause/reason with past tense verbs: 雨が降ったために (ame ga futta tame ni, 'because it rained').

name: 〜たらいい (tara ii: it would be nice if; should)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine the たら (tara) conditional with いい (ii, 'good') to express 'it would be nice if' or to give gentle advice: 'you should just...'

Example from this song: 泣いたらいい (naitara ii) = 'it's fine to cry / you should just cry' — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣いたら (naitara) + いい (ii). Also: 笑えたらいい (waraetara ii) = 'it would be nice if I could laugh'

More examples:
• どうしたらいい？ (dou shitara ii, 'what should I do?') — very common question
• 休んだらいい (yasundara ii, 'you should rest') — from 休む (yasumu, 'to rest')
• 素直に言ったらいい (sunao ni ittara ii, 'you should just say it honestly')

Note: たらいい gives softer advice than べき (beki). As a question (どうしたらいい?), it's one of the most useful phrases for asking 'what should I do?' The potential form + たらいい expresses a wish.
って is the casual contraction of と (quotative) or は/というのは (topic). 先入観って 'speaking of preconceptions'; 〜って言って 'saying X'. Context tells you which sense applies. Pervasive in everyday speech.
explanation.es: って es la contracción casual de と (citativo) o は/というのは (tópico). 先入観って 'hablando de prejuicios'; 〜って言って 'diciendo X'. El contexto indica el sentido. Muy frecuente.
explanation.pt-BR: って é contração casual de と (quotativo) ou は/というのは (tópico). 先入観って 'falando de preconceitos'; 〜って言って 'dizendo X'. Contexto indica o sentido. Pervasivo no falar.

name: 〜てみせる (te miseru) — I'll show you I can!

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + みせる (miseru, "to show") expresses strong determination — "I will definitely do ~ (and prove it)!" or "I'll show you that I can ~!" It is a declaration of resolve. Literally, it means "I will do ~ and show (the result)." This is a powerful, confident expression.

Example from this song:
The singer declares with conviction that they will achieve something and prove it to the world.

More examples:
• 絶対に勝ってみせる (zettai ni katte miseru) — "I will win, I'll show you!"
• 夢を叶えてみせる (yume o kanaete miseru) — "I will make my dream come true, just watch!"
• 最後まで生き延びてみせる (saigo made ikinobite miseru) — "I'll survive to the end, I promise!"

How it works: Add てやる (te yaru) after the te-form of a verb to express doing something with determination, defiance, or for someone else (in a rough/masculine way). It shows a strong, aggressive resolve.

Example from this song: The song uses てやる to convey fierce determination — 'I'll definitely do it!' with a defiant edge.

More examples:
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見てやる (mite yaru, 'I'll show you / I'll see it through')
• 倒す (taosu, 'to defeat') → 倒してやる (taoshite yaru, 'I'll take you down!')
• 勝つ (katsu, 'to win') → 勝ってやる (katte yaru, 'I'll win, just watch!')

Note: てやる is masculine and assertive. It can mean 'do something for someone' (condescending) or 'I'll definitely do it' (determined). The polite equivalent for doing favors is てあげる (te ageru).

name: 〜ではなくて (de wa nakute: not X, but)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + ではなくて (de wa nakute) or the casual じゃなくて (ja nakute) to negate one thing and introduce another — 'not X, but rather Y'.

Example from this song: 景色じゃなくて (keshiki ja nakute) = 'not the scenery, but...' — from 景色 (keshiki, 'scenery') + じゃなくて (ja nakute, 'not, but') → followed by 眩しさを (mabushisa wo, 'the brightness')

More examples:
• 嘘 (uso, 'lie') → 嘘じゃなくて本当 (uso ja nakute hontou, 'not a lie, but the truth')
• お金 (okane, 'money') → お金じゃなくて時間 (okane ja nakute jikan, 'not money, but time')
• 悲しい (kanashii, 'sad') → 悲しいんじゃなくて寂しい (kanashii n ja nakute sabishii, 'not sad, but lonely')

Note: じゃなくて is casual; ではなくて is formal. This pattern clarifies what you really mean — correcting a possible misunderstanding. Very useful in daily conversation.

How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -anai. For ichidan verbs, drop る and add ない. This creates the plain negative — 'not do'.

Example from this song: 負けない (makenai) = 'won't lose' — from 負ける (makeru, 'to lose') → drop る, add ない → 負けない

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かない (ikanai, 'won't go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べない (tabenai, 'won't eat')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しない (shinai, 'won't do')

Note: Combined with ぞ (zo) in the song as 負けないぞ — the ぞ adds strong masculine emphasis, like 'I absolutely won't lose!'
explanation.es:
Cómo funciona: Para verbos godan, cambia el -u final a -anai. Para verbos ichidan, quita る y agrega ない.

Ejemplo: 負けない (makenai) = 'no perderé' — de 負ける → 負けない
explanation.pt-BR:
Como funciona: Para verbos godan, mude o -u final para -anai. Para verbos ichidan, tire る e adicione ない.

Exemplo: 負けない (makenai) = 'não vou perder' — de 負ける → 負けない

explanation.en:
How it works: なき (naki) is the classical/literary form of ない (nai, 'without/not'), used to modify nouns. It gives a poetic, timeless quality.

Example from this song: 終わりなき (owari naki) = 'endless / without end' — from 終わり (owari, 'end') + なき (naki, literary 'without')

More examples:
• 果てなき旅 (hate naki tabi, 'an endless journey') — from 果て (hate, 'end')
• 名もなき花 (na mo naki hana, 'a nameless flower') — from 名 (na, 'name')
• 限りなき愛 (kagiri naki ai, 'limitless love') — from 限り (kagiri, 'limit')

Note: なき is the literary equivalent of ない used as an adjective. Modern Japanese would say 終わりのない (owari no nai). なき appears in song titles, poetry, and formal writing for its elegance.

How it works: なき is the classical (archaic) attributive form of the negative adjective 〜ない. It attaches before a noun to mean 'without X' or 'X-less'. In modern Japanese, you'd use 〜のない, but classical なき lingers in literary, lyrical, and idiomatic use.

Examples from this song:
• 中身なき人間 (nakami naki ningen) = 'humans without substance'
• 誓いのなき百鬼夜行 (chikai no naki hyakki yakō) = 'a demon parade without vows'

More examples (idiomatic / literary):
• 信じて疑わぬ (shinjite utagawanu) = 'believe without doubting' (same classical pattern)
• 声なき声 (koe naki koe) = 'a voiceless voice'
• 限りなき夢 (kagiri naki yume) = 'a limitless dream'

Note: Eve heavily uses classical/literary Japanese to evoke mystical and poetic weight — なき, 在る, 紡ぐ all share that elevated register. Modern speech would say 中身のない人間 instead.
explanation.es:
Cómo funciona: なき es la forma atributiva clásica (arcaica) de 〜ない. Se coloca antes de un sustantivo para significar 'sin X'. En japonés moderno usaríamos 〜のない, pero なき perdura en el uso literario, lírico e idiomático.

Ejemplos de la canción:
• 中身なき人間 = 'humanos sin sustancia'
• 誓いのなき百鬼夜行 = 'un desfile de demonios sin juramentos'

Más ejemplos (idiomáticos/literarios):
• 声なき声 = 'una voz sin voz'
• 限りなき夢 = 'un sueño sin límites'
• 跡形なき = 'sin rastro'

Nota: Eve utiliza mucho el japonés clásico/literario para evocar peso místico y poético — なき, 在る, 紡ぐ comparten ese registro elevado. El habla moderna diría 中身のない人間.
explanation.pt-BR:
Como funciona: なき é a forma atributiva clássica (arcaica) de 〜ない. Liga-se antes de um substantivo para significar 'sem X'. No japonês moderno, usaríamos 〜のない, mas なき permanece no uso literário, lírico e idiomático.

Exemplos da música:
• 中身なき人間 = 'humanos sem substância'
• 誓いのなき百鬼夜行 = 'um desfile de demônios sem juramentos'

Mais exemplos (idiomáticos/literários):
• 声なき声 = 'uma voz sem voz'
• 限りなき夢 = 'um sonho ilimitado'
• 跡形なき (atokata naki) = 'sem vestígio'

Nota: Eve usa muito o japonês clássico/literário para evocar peso místico e poético — なき, 在る, 紡ぐ pertencem ao mesmo registro elevado. A fala moderna diria 中身のない人間.

explanation.en:
〜ぬ is the classical Japanese equivalent of 〜ない — the negative ending of verbs. It survives in modern Japanese in literary texts, lyrics, formal phrases, and a few set expressions. When used attributively (modifying a noun) it tends to feel stately or poetic.

This song uses 見ぬ in three parallel verses: まだ見ぬヒカリ, まだ見ぬチカラ, まだ見ぬタカラ. Each modifies a noun with 'still-unseen' weight that the colloquial 見ていない could not match.

For most verbs, the form is verb (negative stem) + ぬ: 知らぬ ('not knowing'), 行かぬ ('not going'), 見ぬ ('not seen'). する becomes せぬ. The set phrase 〜ねばならぬ ('must do') is another common holdover. Other typical examples: 知らぬ顔 ('a face that doesn't know — feigned ignorance'), 動かぬ証拠 ('immovable evidence'), 言わぬが花 ('it's better not to say').

How it works: Add のだろう (no darou) after a verb or adjective to express wondering or speculation — 'I wonder if...' or 'probably...'. It combines the explanatory の (no) with だろう (darou, conjecture).

Example from this song: 別れたのだろう (wakareta no darou) = 'I wonder if they parted' — from 別れた (wakareta, 'parted') + のだろう (no darou, 'I wonder')

More examples:
• 知っている (shitteiru, 'know') → 知っているのだろう (shitteiru no darou, 'I wonder if they know')
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来るのだろう (kuru no darou, 'will they come, I wonder')
• 本当 (hontou, 'true') → 本当なのだろう (hontou na no darou, 'is it really true, I wonder')

Note: だろう alone is conjecture ('probably'). Adding の before it creates a more reflective, wondering tone. Often used in song lyrics for rhetorical questions.

name: 〜ばいい (ba ii: just do; should do)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine the ば conditional form with いい (ii, 'good') to express 'you should just do X' or 'it would be good if X.' It gives advice or suggests a simple solution.

Example from this song: 追い続ければいい (oitsuzukereba ii) = 'you should just keep chasing' — from 追い続ける (oitsuzukeru, 'to keep chasing') → 追い続ければ (oitsuzukereba) + いい (ii)

More examples:
• 聞けばいい (kikeba ii, 'you should just ask') — from 聞く (kiku, 'to ask')
• 行けばいい (ikeba ii, 'you should just go') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• 何を食べればいい？ (nani o tabereba ii, 'what should I eat?') — as a question, 'what should I...?'

Note: As a statement, ばいい gives casual advice. As a question (どうすればいい?), it asks 'what should I do?' This is one of the most practical patterns for everyday conversation.

How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add やしない (ya shinai). This is an emphatic colloquial negative meaning 'can't possibly' or 'won't even'. It adds emotional frustration or strong denial.

Example from this song: できやしない (deki ya shinai) = 'can't possibly do it' — from できる (dekiru, 'can do') → でき (deki, masu-stem) + やしない (ya shinai, emphatic negative)

More examples:
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かりやしない (wakari ya shinai, 'won't understand at all')
• 売れる (ureru, 'to sell') → 売れやしない (ure ya shinai, 'won't sell at all')
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来やしない (ki ya shinai, 'won't come at all')

Note: This is casual and emotional. The や adds emphasis to the negation. You'll hear it when someone is frustrated or dismissive.

name: 〜ようと (you to) — no matter what / regardless

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb volitional form + と (to) or とも (tomo) means "no matter what ~" or "regardless of ~." It expresses that whatever may happen, the result will be the same. The volitional form sets up the hypothetical, and と (to) dismisses its relevance. This is a formal, determined expression.

Example from this song:
待ち受けていようと (machiukete iyou to) — "no matter what awaits"
Whatever challenges may lie ahead, the singer faces them undeterred.

More examples:
• 何があろうと (nani ga arou to) — "no matter what happens"
• 誰が反対しようと (dare ga hantai shiyou to) — "no matter who opposes"
• どんな困難が来ようとも (donna konnan ga koyou tomo) — "no matter what difficulty comes"

How it works: Combine the explanatory ん (n) with だろう (darou, conjecture). This creates 'you probably...' or 'I wonder if...'. It's the explanatory version of だろう.

Example from this song: 気付いているんだろう (kizuiteiru ndarou) = 'you've probably noticed' — from 気付いている (kizuiteiru, 'have noticed') + んだろう (ndarou, 'probably')

More examples:
• 知っている (shitteiru, 'know') → 知ってるんだろう (shitterundarou, 'you probably know')
• 好き (suki, 'like') → 好きなんだろう (suki nandarou, 'you probably like it')
• 辛い (tsurai, 'painful') → 辛いんだろう (tsuraiundarou, 'it's probably painful')

Note: Without ん: だろう = simple conjecture ('probably'). With ん: んだろう = reflective wondering with explanatory nuance ('I suppose the reason is...'). Common in introspective song lyrics.

name: 〜フリをする (furi wo suru: to pretend)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use [state/action] + フリをする (furi wo suru) to express pretending — 'to act as if' or 'to pretend to be'. フリ means 'pretense' or 'act'.

Example from this song: 気にならないフリして (ki ni naranai furi shite) = 'pretending not to care' — from 気にならない (ki ni naranai, 'don't care') + フリ (furi, 'pretense') + して (shite, 'doing')

More examples:
• 知る (shiru, 'to know') → 知らないフリをする (shiranai furi wo suru, 'to pretend not to know')
• 寝る (neru, 'to sleep') → 寝たフリをする (neta furi wo suru, 'to pretend to be sleeping')
• 元気 (genki, 'fine') → 元気なフリをする (genki na furi wo suru, 'to pretend to be fine')

Note: フリ is often written in katakana to stand out, though 振り is the kanji form. This pattern beautifully captures the song's theme of hiding true feelings — putting on an act to mask vulnerability.

How it works: けして (keshite) or 決して (keshite) combined with a negative verb means 'never' or 'by no means.' It creates an emphatic absolute negation.

Example from this song: The song uses けして...ない to express something that will absolutely never happen — an unbreakable resolve.

More examples:
• 決して忘れない (keshite wasurenai, 'I will never forget') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')
• 決して諦めない (keshite akiramenai, 'I will never give up') — from 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up')
• 決して許さない (keshite yurusanai, 'I will never forgive') — from 許す (yurusu, 'to forgive')

Note: 決して must always pair with a negative form. Never use it with positive verbs. It's stronger than ぜんぜん〜ない (zenzen ~nai, 'not at all'). 決して expresses firm determination.

How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -ou. For ichidan verbs, replace る with よう. For する, it becomes しよう (shiyou). This expresses 'let's do' or 'I shall do'.

Example from this song: しよう (shiyou) = 'let's do' — from する (suru, 'to do') → しよう (shiyou)

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行こう (ikou, 'let's go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べよう (tabeyou, 'let's eat')
• 始める (hajimeru, 'to begin') → 始めよう (hajimeyou, 'let's begin')

Note: The volitional can express invitation ('let's...'), personal resolve ('I shall...'), or suggestion ('why don't we...'). In songs, it often conveys determination and forward movement.

い-adjective stem + さ creates abstract nouns: 悔しい → 悔しさ ('frustration'), 寂しい → 寂しさ ('loneliness'), 強い → 強さ ('strength'), 大きい → 大きさ ('size'). Highly productive — works on virtually all い-adjectives and most な-adjectives.
explanation.es: Raíz de adjetivo い + さ forma sustantivos abstractos: 悔しい → 悔しさ, 寂しい → 寂しさ, 強い → 強さ, 大きい → 大きさ. Patrón muy productivo.
explanation.pt-BR: Raiz de adjetivo い + さ cria substantivos abstratos: 悔しい → 悔しさ, 寂しい → 寂しさ, 強い → 強さ, 大きい → 大きさ. Padrão muito produtivo.

explanation.en:
Sentence-ending particles used in casual, masculine speech. They add emphasis, energy, or a tough/playful tone.

How it works:
ぞ (zo) adds strong assertion or warning. ぜ (ze) adds confident emphasis. Both are informal and mostly used by male speakers.

Example from this song:
内緒だぞ (naisho da zo, "It’s a secret!" - playful, rough)

More examples:
- 行くぞ (iku zo, "Let’s go!" - assertive)
- やるぜ (yaru ze, "I’m gonna do it!" - confident)
- すごいぞ (sugoi zo, "That’s amazing!" - excited)

Causative: negative stem + せる (godan: 書く → 書かせる) or 〜させる (ichidan: 食べる → 食べさせる). Can mean 'make someone do' or 'let someone do'.

From this song: 火山を爆発させる = 'make the volcanoes erupt' — 爆発する → 爆発させる.

More examples:
• 弟を泣かせた (I made my brother cry.)
• 考えさせて (Let me think.)
• 休ませる (Let rest.)

い-adjectives in Classical Japanese take 〜き when modifying a noun: 美しい → 美しき, 愛しい → 愛しき, 儚い → 儚き, 強い → 強き. Used in lyrics, titles, poetry for an archaic/elevated tone. Don't use in regular conversation.
explanation.es: Los adjetivos い en japonés clásico llevan 〜き al modificar un sustantivo: 美しい → 美しき, 愛しい → 愛しき, 儚い → 儚き, 強い → 強き. En letras, títulos, poesía.
explanation.pt-BR: Adjetivos い no japonês clássico levam 〜き ao modificar substantivo: 美しい → 美しき, 愛しい → 愛しき, 儚い → 儚き, 強い → 強き. Em letras, títulos, poesia.

explanation.en:
How it works:
A conditional sentence with "if" sets up a condition and its result. The First Conditional (if + present, will + base verb) covers real or likely situations. The Second Conditional (if + past, would + base verb) handles hypothetical or unlikely ones. In song lyrics, conditionals create emotional stakes — "what if this happens?"

Example from this song:
"If I lose it all" — a real conditional presenting a plausible, terrifying scenario. The singer contemplates the possibility of losing everything and what emotional state would follow.

More examples:
• "If the walls fall, we fall with them" — real condition tied to a consequence
• "If I had wings, I would fly away" — hypothetical (Second Conditional)
• "If you leave, nothing remains" — condition with devastating result

真っ + adjective is an emphatic prefix meaning 'completely / dead-X': 真っ白 ('pure white'), 真っ赤 ('deep red'), 真っ黒 ('jet black'), 真っ暗 ('pitch dark'), 真っ直ぐ ('straight'). Highly productive — pairs with most adjectives describing total saturation.
explanation.es: 真っ + adjetivo es prefijo enfático que significa 'completamente X': 真っ白, 真っ赤, 真っ黒, 真っ暗, 真っ直ぐ. Muy productivo.
explanation.pt-BR: 真っ + adjetivo é prefixo enfático que significa 'completamente X': 真っ白, 真っ赤, 真っ黒, 真っ暗, 真っ直ぐ. Muito produtivo.

name: Emphatic は in negative: 〜たくはない

explanation.en: Inserting は in a negative form adds emphasis/contrast: 知りたくない ('don't want to know') → 知りたくはない ('I particularly don't want to know'). The は singles out the verb as the un-wanted thing.
explanation.es: Insertar は en una forma negativa añade énfasis/contraste: 知りたくない → 知りたくはない ('precisamente no quiero saberlo'). La は singulariza el verbo como lo NO deseado.
explanation.pt-BR: Inserir は numa forma negativa enfatiza/contrasta: 知りたくない → 知りたくはない ('especificamente não quero saber'). O は destaca o verbo como aquilo que NÃO se quer.

explanation.en:
This song is entirely in German. It is one of the most iconic emotional pieces in Attack on Titan, reflecting themes of mortality, beauty, and fighting against fate.

The vocabulary section is empty for this track because the German lyrics do not map directly to beginner Japanese grammar. However, key concepts from this song have Japanese equivalents:
- Leben (life) = 命 (inochi) or 人生 (jinsei)
- Schicksal (fate) = 運命 (unmei)
- Licht (light) = 光 (hikari)
- Kinder (children) = 子供たち (kodomo-tachi)

Bare imperative for blunt orders. u-verbs replace -u with -e: 掴み取る → 掴み取れ ('seize!'), 描き出す → 描き出せ ('draw it out!'). ru-verbs replace -る with -ろ: 食べる → 食べろ. Irregulars: する → しろ, 来る → 来い. Linked Horizon stacks two imperatives at the song's chorus and finale: 掴み取れ at verse 3, 描き出せ at the closing verse. Same energy as 'seize the day' delivered as a military order.
explanation.es: Imperativo directo para órdenes tajantes. Verbos-u cambian -u por -e: 掴み取る → 掴み取れ ('¡agarra!'), 描き出す → 描き出せ ('¡dibújalo!'). Verbos-ru cambian -る por -ろ: 食べる → 食べろ. Irregulares: する → しろ, 来る → 来い. Linked Horizon apila dos imperativos en el estribillo y el final: 掴み取れ en el verso 3, 描き出せ en el verso de cierre. Misma energía que 'toma el día' dada como orden militar.
explanation.pt-BR: Imperativo direto pra ordens secas. Verbos-u trocam -u por -e: 掴み取る → 掴み取れ ('agarre!'), 描き出す → 描き出せ ('desenhe!'). Verbos-ru trocam -る por -ろ: 食べる → 食べろ. Irregulares: する → しろ, 来る → 来い. Linked Horizon empilha dois imperativos no refrão e no final: 掴み取れ no verso 3, 描き出せ no verso de fechamento. Mesma energia de 'tome o dia' entregue como ordem militar.

explanation.en: 〜ぬ is the classical negative ending equivalent to 〜ない: 隠せぬ = 隠せない ('cannot hide'), 満たせぬ = 満たせない ('cannot be filled'). Common in lyrics, set phrases (時の流れに身をまかせぬ), and proverbs. Reads as more solemn or old-fashioned.
explanation.es: 〜ぬ es la terminación negativa clásica equivalente a 〜ない: 隠せぬ = 隠せない, 満たせぬ = 満たせない. Frecuente en letras, frases hechas y proverbios. Suena más solemne/antiguo.
explanation.pt-BR: 〜ぬ é a terminação negativa clássica equivalente a 〜ない: 隠せぬ = 隠せない, 満たせぬ = 満たせない. Comum em letras, expressões fixas e provérbios. Soa mais solene/antigo.
